condition.label: lumbar radicular pain
condition.distinctions: Radicular pain is nerve-root-related pain; referred leg pain and radiculopathy with objective neurological loss are overlapping but distinct populations.

scope.population: Ages 18–60, recent sciatica under 90 days; Acute sciatica in general practice
scope.stage: Varies by source; acute/recent versus chronic and symptom irritability are explicitly retained. Unknown stage remains unknown.
scope.operativeStatus: Nonsurgical evidence predominates; no postoperative protocol approved or inferred.
scope.exclusions: Source-specific exclusions are applicability boundaries, not diagnosis-wide contraindications. Coexisting conditions and independently selected joint limits retain precedence.
scope.uncertainty:
- Ordinary training: high-irritability stage needs clinician-defined tolerable activity/progression; worsening neurological symptoms must stop automated escalation and trigger assessment. Persistent or progressive deficit requires a clinical pathway, not substitution to “fill” a workout. LR-G1 supports this clinical boundary; LR-P1 supports assessed directional response, not diagnosis-only extension assignment.
- Supportive candidates: clinician-selected directional movement, graded general conditioning/strengthening. Directional preference/centralization must be supplied by assessment; unknown is unknown. No fixed flexion or extension prohibition, nerve-tension dosage or heavy-lifting ceiling is established.
- Restriction-only draft is defensible while symptom stage/directional response are unknown. Actual release requires a usable, clinically reviewed rule and compatible catalog execution. No direct comparative primary study retrieved establishes that all squats, deadlifts or stretches worsen lumbar radicular pain.
- Search gap: 2025 chronic lumbar radicular self-management scoping review located (ScienceDirect S2468781225001122), full text not inspected. No dosing inference drawn.

sources.design: Final KNGF evidence-based physical therapy guideline
sources.population: Adults with low-back pain/lumbosacral radicular syndrome without red flags; severe neurological presentations/recent surgery outside scope
sources.coInterventions: Advice, education, risk stratification and shared decision making
sources.outcomes: Apeldoorn et al., KNGF guideline, 2024 final. DOI 10.23736/S1973-9087.24.08352-7, PMID 38407016, PMC11112513; FT via Europe PMC XML. Adults LBP/lumbosacral radicular syndrome without red flags. Activity/exercise progression depends pain/irritability: avoid increasing pain in high irritability; brief increase may be acceptable in moderate irritability. This is individualized guidance, not a fixed joint angle cap. Immediate physician contact advised for saddle numbness, bowel/bladder changes or increasing leg weakness. Severe neurological cases and recent surgery fall outside guideline scope; that scope limit is not itself a trial-proven contraindication. No universal flexion/extension or lifting exclusion established.
sources.uncertainty: Irritability-specific guidance requires assessment; scope exclusions are not proof of universal exercise harm
sources.harms: Harms evidence varies; table VII specifies immediate-contact neurological symptoms
sources.limitations: Irritability-specific guidance requires assessment; scope exclusions are not proof of universal exercise harm Trial exclusions delimit studied applicability; they do not establish general contraindications.

protocol.dose: No fixed execution-level dose; table VIII suggests prior activity level over 6–12 weeks when progress permits
protocol.supervision: Physical therapist assessment and shared decision making
protocol.progression: High irritability: pain alleviation/prevent increase; moderate: short-lived increase may be acceptable
protocol.stoppingRules: Immediate GP contact for saddle numbness, unintended bowel/urine loss/inability to urinate, increasing leg weakness; table VII

sources.comparator: Education alone versus education plus early physical therapy
sources.coInterventions: Manual therapy plus individualized directional exercise
sources.outcomes: Fritz et al., 2021 (online 2020) pragmatic RCT. DOI 10.7326/M20-4187, PMID 33017565, PMC7856080. FT. 220 adults 18–60, recent sciatica <90 days. Education versus education plus 4-week PT including individualized directional exercise/manual therapy (recommended 6–8 visits; home exercise every 4–5 hours). Disability advantage at 6 months −5.4/100 (95% CI −9.4 to −1.3); at one year −4.8 (−8.9 to −0.7); no health-care-use/work-loss difference. Thirty-seven PT recipients reported 133 effects, commonly back pain/stiffness; 13 effects severe in intensity, seven persisted >24 h. Movements chosen to centralize symptoms; extension often used, never automatically for all. Cannot isolate exercise from manual therapy or establish an unsupervised gym prescription.

sources.uncertainty: Package effects cannot isolate exercise; directional response assessed clinically

sources.population: Mixed low-back-related leg pain including referred pain; 212 recruited in body versus 196 analyzed in abstract
sources.comparator: One versus two sets; individualized functional restoration versus advice
sources.outcomes: Barbari et al., 2024 systematic review. DOI 10.7759/cureus.57278, PMID 38559546, PMC10981532; FT via XML. Two resistance-training RCTs; abstract reports 196 analyzed participants, body 212 recruited. Mixed low-back-related leg pain, including referred pain, not a homogeneous confirmed radiculopathy cohort. One versus two sets showed no clear difference; individual functional restoration versus advice yielded limited/mixed superiority. No serious adverse events reported; optimal dose/long-term superiority uncertain. Cannot turn these mixed-population findings into radiculopathy-specific load ceilings or assume neural “flossing” is equivalent to strength training.
sources.uncertainty: Not a homogeneous confirmed radiculopathy cohort; optimal dose uncertain
sources.harms: No serious adverse events reported in included studies; not proof of universal safety
sources.limitations: Not a homogeneous confirmed radiculopathy cohort; optimal dose uncertain Trial exclusions delimit studied applicability; they do not establish general contraindications.
